data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), not probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' implicitly relies on the assumption that the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' secretly presupposes inductive reliability of background knowledge.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven and improbable) and the rational basis for preferring one theory over another for practical application. The mechanism is 'critical preference': we prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it has shown greater capacity to survive falsification attempts, suggesting it is closer to the truth (higher verisimilitude), even if we cannot assign it a higher probability. This is a decision rule, not an inductive inference.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
